extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, academic authors, and journal editors (mathematics community)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for submitting, reviewing, and publishing mathematical research (including computational experiments, editorial policies, and journal management). Targets authors, referees, and editors in mathematics and adjacent fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do computer experiments and share results
rubrics_metrics.description: Please do try computer experiments for whatever you are working on. Make an effort to think it through and design a good experiment. Work hard to test as much as your computer technology allows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need computing power, ask around (university resources, private donations). If you succeed, write a paper and publish it; make your code and work notes publicly available. If you fail, do exactly the same — keep it on the arXiv if journals refuse to publish. Treat computational work (and failures) as 'work product' deserving credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standard for mathematical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical journals tend to prefer 100% correctness over probabilistic high-confidence evidence; a 'five sigma' style counterexample tested computationally is usually insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monte Carlo testing can confirm an inequality with high probability but cannot formally disprove a conjecture. Authors should aim for formal combinatorial or deductive proofs when possible; journals typically require certainty rather than high-probability empirical evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to house style and strict format limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions to APS journals are required to be in a house two-column style with a tiny font; there are sharp word count limits for 'letters' and 'articles'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting and word-count issues (how to count formulas/tables) are annoying but important — poor adherence can lead to desk rejection by non-expert editors. Make an effort to follow style guidelines closely to avoid avoidable rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, brevity, and readable style
rubrics_metrics.description: Good style is emphasized; papers in physics tend to be shorter and more readable compared with the average math paper. Brevity is a feature, not a bug.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overlong papers when possible; clear presentation helps avoid desk rejection and improves referee accessibility. Editors pay attention to style as part of initial screening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and design for editorial screening (desk rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: About 15–20% of PRE papers are rejected within days after initial screening by managing or associate editors; desk rejection protects reviewer resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare submissions to survive quick screening: clear abstract, readable presentation, correct format, and appropriately targeted scope. Don't expect desk rejection rates to be negligible—match scope and quality to journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness expectations for review process
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are typically asked for three-week reports; editors aim to finish the first round in three months and publish within about six months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design revisions and respond promptly to meet these timelines. Editors may extend reviewer deadlines by a few weeks but not months. Long delays often stem from difficulty finding referees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals and editorial oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: When a paper is rejected, authors have the right to appeal; the paper is sent to a member of the Editorial Board who reads the paper and referee reports and writes a signed report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals serve as an important community check on associate editors. Note that many math journals lack a formal appeals process; authors should be aware of a journal's appeals policy before submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial transparency and accessible logs
rubrics_metrics.description: The APS editorial system allows authors to see a complete log of dates, anonymized referees, and editor actions, offering an unprecedented level of transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent workflows help authors track progress and provide accountability. Authors and editors should favor systems that expose process logs and communications (anonymized) where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team-based editorial management
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors work as a team, jointly handling incoming email and submission/resubmission traffic; routine tasks are handled by the first available person, while decisions are made by the assigned Associate Editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Team workflows and queue redistribution for backlogged editors improve speed and consistency. Journals should adopt team practices to avoid single-point failures and long delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-journal coordination and transfer of submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: APS editors can see actions and reports across journals; rejected papers at one title can be invited to another (e.g., PRL→PRE), speeding decisions and reusing reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfers save reviewer resources and accelerate publication when scope differs between sibling journals. Authors should consider this pathway and journals should enable safe cross-journal transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance/selectivity aligned with journal mission
rubrics_metrics.description: Different journals have different acceptance rates (PRE ~55–60%, PRL ~20–25%, Nature/Science much lower); acceptance ratios reflect scope and editorial goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should match paper significance, length, and style to journal selectivity; journals should be explicit about their mission (rapid community service vs highly selective novelty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-acceptance production speed and zero backlog
rubrics_metrics.description: At PRE, production (outsourced) typically produces online publication within 2–3 weeks of acceptance and there is zero backlog.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fast production is a desirable journal attribute — quick turnaround after acceptance benefits authors and readers. Authors should follow proofing instructions promptly to keep timelines short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and incentives for referees
rubrics_metrics.description: APS instituted an Outstanding Referee Award to encourage quick and thorough refereeing, selecting a small number of awardees annually based on nominations by Associate Editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should have mechanisms to recognize excellent reviewing (awards, plaques, formal acknowledgment) to incentivize timely, high-quality referee reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation and support for survey/expository work
rubrics_metrics.description: APS publishes Reviews of Modern Physics and solicits surveys/perspectives, offering modest honoraria to incentivize completion on schedule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should actively solicit and support expository work (surveys, perspectives) and consider compensating or prioritizing such contributions to improve community exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial highlighting as minor awards
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Editors’ Suggestions' or similar profiled articles serve as minor research awards and are publicly highlighted by the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorially highlighted papers provide recognition for authors and can be listed on CVs; journals can use such mechanisms to signal noteworthy contributions beyond formal acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: ArXiv-friendly submission policy
rubrics_metrics.description: APS encourages submissions that include arXiv numbers and subject areas; unlike Nature/Science, APS accepts arXiv-posted preprints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should prefer journals that allow or encourage arXiv preprints if they want rapid dissemination; journals should clarify their arXiv policies to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility: publish code and explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: When computational methods are used, make source code and explanations available (e.g., GitHub) to allow replication and verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public code and documentation increase trust, allow others to reproduce experiments, and help the community validate computational results even if formal proofs are required later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission and appeal fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals allow resubmissions of previously rejected papers, but resubmissions often go to the same editor, which can defeat the purpose of appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should design resubmission/appeal policies that avoid rubber-stamping past decisions (e.g., consider routing to different editors or panels for fairness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate correctness validation from novelty selection (mega-journal idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed 'mega journal' would check validity/correctness only (publish based on correctness), while separate venues or awards would handle novelty/importance selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separating the tasks could speed verification, reduce repeated submissions, and allow competitive awards or overlay journals to handle prestige. This model suggests a central correctness-checking service and independent selection/award mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlay journal / baby-mega competition model
rubrics_metrics.description: Overlay journals could link to arXiv-hosted papers and 'bid' for the best papers (like admissions); authors accept the best bid and the paper is linked to the journal in an arXiv-overlay style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates competition for highlighting work without duplicating peer-review effort, and could reduce pressure on traditional journals; journals/publishers should consider overlay or baby-mega architectures to improve selection fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-oriented editorial stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should validate significance, help authors improve style, be friendly to newcomers, and not unduly second-guess experimental findings; operate as a service to the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A community-minded approach (rapid turnaround, constructive feedback, reasonable acceptance thresholds) fosters goodwill and better scientific discourse compared to adversarial or opaque editorial cultures.
